A build-along course

Building Meridian

A trip planner for people who travel together: pins from everybody on one map, a globe that flies the route, days you can drag, expenses split to the cent, notes that save themselves, invites, and three languages — built from an empty folder as a pnpm workspace with a library you could publish. It uses everything Svelte 5 and SvelteKit 3.1.0 offer as of October 2026, and it goes out into the ecosystem on purpose: Bits UI, svelte-maplibre, Threlte, TanStack Table, LayerChart, Tiptap, svelte-dnd-action, Paraglide, Better Auth, runed, mdsvex, enhanced-img — each chosen against alternatives, and each with the reason written down.

Everything we'll cover

  1. 01 What we are building Meridian: a trip planner for people who travel together — a map, a globe, an itinerary you can drag, expenses split to the cent, notes, invites, three languages, a library you could publish, and a second person planning beside you.
  2. 02 A workspace of two The app at the root, the library it publishes in packages/waypoint, and the pnpm settings that make a workspace safe: workspace:*, allowBuilds, a minimum release age, and a prepare script that builds the library before the app can import it.
  3. 03 The toolchain: sv, the checks, and the agent beside you The tools around the code. The sv CLI that scaffolds a project and adds integrations to it, and the one line that reproduces this project’s tooling; svelte-check and every flag worth knowing; ESLint and Prettier; and the Svelte AI tools — instructions, an MCP server, skills and a subagent — with a script that runs the autofixer over every component on every build.
  4. 04 One file to configure everything SvelteKit 3 keeps its whole configuration inside the Vite plugin. This chapter reads vite.config.ts top to bottom: plugin order, mdsvex as a preprocessor, per-file compiler options for the custom element, the inspector, the adapter, remote functions and the three namespaces called experimental, tracing, prerendering, the Content Security Policy, versioning and preloads in a header, Paraglide, and the two test projects — then tsconfig.json, and the options this project leaves at their defaults.
  5. 05 The map: every feature, every library, and where it lives A reference chapter. Every Svelte 5 and SvelteKit 3 feature the project uses, every ecosystem library it reaches for, and the chapter where each one is built and explained — so you can read the course in order or jump to the thing you came for.
  6. 06 Geodesy for humans Distances, bearings, destinations, great-circle interpolation, arcs that survive the date line, bounds and compass points — on a sphere, in metres, with conventions written down. Plain TypeScript with no Svelte in it, so anybody can use it.
  7. 07 A route as a class, in a library Route is an ordered list of waypoints as $state, with legs, total, bounds and the longest leg as $derived. It lives in a .svelte.ts file inside a published package, and it works in the consumer exactly as it works here.
  8. 08 Two components for any app A compass needle and a sparkline: a few dozen lines each, role="img" with an accessible name, props typed with an interface, class forwarded, reduced motion respected. What a library component has to get right that an app component can skip.
  9. 09 Packaging a Svelte library, and proving it svelte-package 3 reads its configuration from Vite, exports draws the line between the framework-free entry and the Svelte one, .js imports name the files that will exist, and publint plus arethetypeswrong check the tarball the way a consumer would.
  10. 10 Ids, dates and money Three small modules that decide three things most apps get wrong: an unguessable slug you can read aloud, a date that is a date and not an instant, and an amount that is an integer of minor units formatted by Intl.
  11. 11 Splitting fairly, to the cent One expense split by weight with the leftover cents handed out by largest remainder; balances per person; and the greedy settlement that pairs the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor. All integers, all deterministic, all tested.
  12. 12 The itinerary as data A stop has a day (or none) and a position within it. groupByDay turns the flat list into the days of the trip plus an ideas bucket; place moves one stop and returns exactly the rows that changed, for the server to write and the browser to apply first.
  13. 13 Schemas with valibot, and who may do what Every remote function takes one of these as its first argument, and SvelteKit validates before the function runs. valibot because it tree-shakes; forward for cross-field checks; picklists that double as the source of truth for the union types; and the two-line roles module.
  14. 14 The database: seven tables and Better Auth’s four The Drizzle schema for trips, members, invites, stops, expenses, shares and notes, with three conventions; Better Auth’s tables kept by hand; one libSQL connection in WAL mode; drizzle-kit for migrations; and a seed that is idempotent.
  15. 15 Environment and hooks src/env.ts declares every variable with a schema; hooks.server.ts composes three handlers with sequence — locale, identity, security — and adds handleFetch, handleError told apart by kind, and init; hooks.client.ts gives the browser’s own failures words; hooks.ts carries reroute and transport to the browser; params.ts matches the slug.
  16. 16 Identity with Better Auth The minimal entry point, configured for email and password with a session cookie cache; sveltekitCookies so a cookie set inside a remote function reaches the response; and access.ts, the three questions every trip function asks and the status codes that give away the least.
  17. 17 Remote functions: the reads query for the trips list and the trip document, query.batch for one preview per card in one request, prerender for a gazetteer written to disk at build time, and the prerendered endpoint that serves the world — with the reason it is an endpoint and not a remote function.
  18. 18 Remote functions: the writes form where a page has a button and must work without JavaScript, command where the action only exists once JavaScript is running; requested().refreshAll() for single-flight updates; invalid() with a field-bound issue; and how a form’s field names carry their types.
  19. 19 Live collaboration: a room, a mailbox and a generator watchTrip is a query.live — an async generator on the server, a .current in the browser — that yields the whole trip and who is looking at it whenever the room is woken. In-process rooms, a one-slot mailbox so a burst becomes one send, presence with a time-to-live, access asked again on every wake, and the two things that end a stream: the abort signal, and a refusal.
  20. 20 Invites and membership An owner makes a single-use, expiring link; a stranger who opens it signs in on the way and joins with the role the link carries — in a transaction, through a form, ending in a redirect. Roles change and members leave the same way.
  21. 21 Three languages with Paraglide Messages as JSON, compiled into one typed function each; plural rules in the message format; a strategy list that decides the locale; reroute and the middleware doing the two halves of /de/trips; and a language switcher that is three links.
  22. 22 Dates, money and distances in a locale Everything that is not interface text: dates and ranges through cached Intl formatters, a headless date range picker that speaks CalendarDate, a transport hook that carries one across the wire, amounts in and out of minor units, and distances in kilometres or miles.
  23. 23 The design system Tokens with light-dark(), a theme class on MediaQuery, the boot script that stops the flash and tells the browser chrome and the server, fonts from fontsource preloaded by filename, a hero in four prints that downloads one, one GSAP timeline as a conditional attachment, motion tokens that reduced motion zeroes and the framework’s one query for the scripts, style:--x as the bridge from a script to the stylesheet, how a component’s styles are scoped, the short, named list of places a hex code may appear outside the tokens, and a contrast table checked on every lint.
  24. 24 Motion with intent What moves in Meridian and what is not allowed to: the design brief’s two lists as the rules, four mechanisms and when each is the right one, the one custom transition with css(t, u), three Svelte transitions and one animate:flip, a Tween for the tab bar, CSS keyframes that Bits UI waits for, a phone menu whose motion ends outside the accessibility tree, the svelte/easing table — and every built-in the project leaves out, with the rule that keeps it out.
  25. 25 The shell: a root that knows nobody The root layout has no header and no load; the (site) group has both; the header computes its links in a {const} declaration tag and reads scrollY from svelte/reactivity/window; view transitions in onNavigate; a version banner from updated.current; two error pages sharing one view.
  26. 26 The trip page: one await, one state object, one stream The page awaits tripBySlug in markup with no boundary; TripView starts the live query and reads props once with untrack; TripState derives everything from whichever snapshot is newer; two presence effects that must not loop; tabs from the URL.
  27. 27 The itinerary: days you can drag One dndzone per day with svelte-dnd-action, animate:flip for the settling, an optimistic override that is derived rather than synced, place() from the domain on both sides, a stop card, a dialog with assignable deriveds that Back closes — a shallow history entry — and a combobox over the gazetteer.
  28. 28 The command palette Ctrl+K: a Dialog around a Command from Bits UI, every stop and every action as an item with a value to match and an onSelect to run, and goto with replace so a tab switch does not fill the history.
  29. 29 The map with no tile server svelte-maplibre over MapLibre GL: a style built from the prerendered world, a worker URL set once in a module script, great-circle legs as a GeoJSON line layer, draggable markers, a theme-following style patched with diffStyleUpdates, and geolocation through createSubscriber.
  30. 30 The globe: Threlte, on demand three.js through Threlte — <T.Mesh> is a mesh, children attach — with coastlines from the same atlas, arcs lifted off the surface, clickable markers, a useTask flyover that follows the library’s great-circle interpolation, a MediaQuery that holds it still, and a dynamic import so three.js reaches only the people who ask for it.
  31. 31 Expenses: a headless table, two charts, and the settle-up TanStack Table v9 with opt-in features and a typed column-meta slot, a get data() getter so the table follows the live document, a small render helper instead of FlexRender, aria-sort on the header; LayerChart for a bar and a pie; the domain’s balances() and settle(); and a remote form whose fields carry their types.
  32. 32 Notes: Tiptap through an attachment Tiptap has no Svelte binding and needs none: {@attach tiptap()} hands it the element and destroys it on cleanup. A debounced command saves the JSON; a counter makes isActive() reactive for the toolbar; remote edits arrive through the live query and are applied only when the person is not mid-sentence.
  33. 33 Companions, presence, the join page and settings The member list with roles and “here now”; the owner’s invite link and two moderation buttons; presence chips fed by the live query; the join page as one query and one form; and the settings page — an owner-only page, a form that reads its props once, single-flight refresh, and a delete that asks first.
  34. 34 Signing in and up Two remote forms, a hidden redirect field the server sanitises, issues() under each input, a group layout that redirects strangers before rendering, and a sign-out that is a form with no fields.
  35. 35 The trips list and a new trip A list awaited in markup with a failed snippet and no pending one; a preview per card through query.batch — two requests for twenty trips; a thumbnail component; and a creation form whose date picker writes hidden inputs named by the form itself, prefilled from the explore page, whose draft survives a reload through snapshot.
  36. 36 Guides: Markdown, prerendered, no JavaScript Four .svx files with validated frontmatter and a Svelte component inside the prose; import.meta.glob to find them; prerender = true and csr = false on the routes; entries for the dynamic one; a chrome that does not know who you are; and the two prerendering errors that shaped the root layout.
  37. 37 Explore, and diagnostics A dynamic page reading prerendered data, debounced with runed, grouped with Intl.DisplayNames, linking with typed resolve(); and a page that reads the server’s own OpenTelemetry spans out of a ring buffer through src/instrumentation.server.ts.
  38. 38 Embedding a trip: a frame and a custom element A JSON endpoint with CORS for link-visible trips only; the one route that may be framed and the CSP override that allows it; <meridian-route> compiled as a custom element by dynamicCompileOptions, built standalone by a second Vite config, previewed on the settings page; and a health endpoint for the machines.
  39. 39 The offline itinerary A service worker for the one scenario the product names — a trip read in a train tunnel: self from $app/service-worker, the build from $app/manifest, the deploy’s version from $app/env, three caching rules and the one the server can veto with no-store; why a remote query is never cached; a separate type-check for a worker; the copies a shared device must forget; a header that says “Offline”; a new worker after a deploy; and an end-to-end suite that waits for the worker instead of the clock.
  40. 40 The survey: what was chosen, what was rejected, and why Every dependency in the project against the four questions from chapter 01, with its version as of October 2026 and the alternatives it beat — and the packages that did not make it, with the reason: not yet on Svelte 5 or SvelteKit 3, folded into the framework, or too heavy for what it did.
  41. 41 The headless pattern: Bits UI and TanStack Table What a headless library gives you and what it asks of you: behaviour, ARIA and keyboard from the library; markup, classes and data from you. Bits UI’s Root/parts structure, bind: on the root, class on every part, portals, snippets with library-provided state; TanStack’s table object with a getter and a render helper.
  42. 42 The wrapper pattern, and when to write an attachment instead svelte-maplibre and Threlte are wrappers: components over an imperative library, mapping a scene or a map onto a template. Tiptap and GSAP are attachments: the library wants one element. The line between them, the costs of each, disposal, per-frame work, and the two things wrappers cannot hide — colours and workers.
  43. 43 Reactivity utilities: svelte/reactivity, runed, and the line between them MediaQuery, createSubscriber and svelte/reactivity/window from the framework; Debounced from runed; the decision about SvelteMap versus a plain Map in a derivation; and the rule for when a utility library earns its line.
  44. 44 Unit and browser tests: two Vitest projects, one command Vitest runs the pure logic in Node and the components in a real Chromium, from one config and one command. The maths and the money get example-based tests with the answers worked out by hand; the components get vitest-browser-svelte, which mounts them and gives back locators that retry. What each layer is for, and what each is not.
  45. 45 What the compiler says: warnings, errors and the codes that name them Every message Svelte prints has a code, and the code is the handle for everything you can do about it. Zero svelte-ignore comments, a check that fails on a warning, and the autofixer in verify; the warnings the code answers by its shape, the errors that explain why it is written the way it is, the runtime errors and warnings worth recognising on sight — and the one warning the build still prints, and why it stays.
  46. 46 End to end: the built server, two viewports, two people Playwright runs against node build/index.js — the same process a deployment runs — on a database rebuilt from the seed before every run, in a desktop and a Pixel 7 profile, and the design’s checks in a third at 360px. Seven suites cover a stranger, an account, one trip’s every tab, the map’s own behaviour, two browsers on one trip, invites plus the embed, and the trip with no network; an eighth asks every screen of the design, in both themes and at three widths, whether anything sticks out, whether a finger can hit it, what axe finds, and how it paints, on a fast connection and a slow one; and a bundle guard after the build holds the chunks to a budget. How the suite is kept honest, what it found, and what each failure taught.
  47. 47 Security: the policy, the headers, the redirect and the one framed route What the server puts on every response and why: a Content Security Policy in auto mode with a hashed boot script, CSRF with no trusted origins, the headers that are always right, Vary: Cookie, a redirect target that is sanitised rather than rejected, a public API whose CORS is safe because its content is, and the single route whose frame policy is loosened per request.
  48. 48 Deploying: three stages, one process, a health check and a pipeline that runs the container The Dockerfile builds the library, the messages, the element and the app in one stage and copies only what running needs into a slim, non-root image whose one process migrates the database and then serves. Compose gives it a volume and a secret. The workflow verifies the project, builds and *runs* the image, and proves the course — because a Dockerfile that is never built is documentation.
  49. 49 Migrating a major: the routine, the record, and a dependency still on Svelte 4 sv migrate and its task-based migrations — one task per commit, @migration-task comments, and a MIGRATION_TASKS.md for what no tool can decide — with the record this project kept, every box resolved. What SvelteKit 3 removed and renamed, module by module and option by option; and how to read a component written for Svelte 4, each legacy construct with its runes replacement and the code that flags it.
  50. 50 What I would do next, and what you now know The project is complete and the suite is green, and it is still version one. An honest list of the next ten pieces of work, each with the chapter it would touch, then every deferred item with the reason it waits — generated, and checked against the exit criteria; a map from every Svelte and SvelteKit capability the course used to the chapter that used it; and how to keep the project current as the framework moves.
  51. 51 The exit criteria: what a DPE 8++ in Svelte can do What “8++” means for this course, measured: every surface the coverage plan assigned to a chapter, with what you should be able to do with it and where it was taught — or declined, deferred or dropped, and why. Twelve production exercises that start where the course stops, a rubric, and the routine that keeps you current.

Every code block in this course is read out of the finished project in meridian at build time — file and line numbers included — so it cannot drift from what the code actually says. Type it out rather than pasting where you can: the errors you make and fix are the part that sticks. Where the project chose a library, the chapter says which alternatives were weighed and why this one won; where it chose not to, it says that too.
